bp: A map assistant is useful only if it can connect a person’s request to live services outside the language model. When someone asks Baidu Map’s AI Guide for something practical, the system may need a map search service, a routing service, a business-hours service, or some newly needed service that was not already wired into the assistant. The language model can read the request, but it cannot by itself fetch fresh map facts unless it knows which application programming interface, or API, to call. ARADD is about keeping that tool supply up to date. As user requests diversify, the system must notice new kinds of intent, find or design APIs that can answer them, and create examples that teach the assistant how to use those APIs. The paper serves a production problem: reduce the human labor and human bias involved in expanding an AI guide service.
wh: The hard part is that new user needs do not arrive as clean labels. They arrive as messy natural requests, often phrased in many different ways, and the system must decide whether they are ordinary variations of known needs or signs that a new service ability is missing. A team could manually inspect logs, name intents, design APIs, and write training pairs, but that creates a bottleneck. It also imports the team’s assumptions about which user needs matter. Automation is risky because a language model may overread a query, invent an intent, choose an API that only partly fits, or generate training data that teaches the agent the wrong habit. The challenge is therefore two-sided: discover real unmet needs from logs while also producing reliable training material for the agent that will later act in front of users.
naive: A smart beginner would start with a catalog of known APIs and a set of hand-written rules: if the query contains restaurant words, call the restaurant API; if it contains route words, call the routing API. When a query cannot be handled, a human would inspect it and add a new rule or request a new API. This works for small services, but it breaks as map queries become diverse. People ask for the same thing with different wording, and different things can share similar words. Manual review is slow, costly, and shaped by what reviewers notice. It also produces limited training data, so the agent may not learn the many ways users express the same intent.
ap: ARADD’s central move is to turn API expansion into a repeated pipeline driven by real user demand. First, it extracts intent, meaning the practical job a user is asking the map assistant to complete. It does this through multiple stages that combine a closed-source language model with a lighter agent, so the heavy model helps identify hard cases while the deployable agent learns the pattern. Second, once a new intent is captured, the system designs or discovers an API suited to that intent in its surrounding context. Third, it creates training pairs by self-instruction: the model produces examples showing how a request for that intent should connect to the API. Finally, a two-stage filtering module keeps the most useful data for fine-tuning the agent, instead of blindly trusting every generated example.
mech: The mechanism starts with query evidence from the map service, especially requests that reveal new or poorly served intents. The first transformation is intent extraction. Instead of treating the user sentence as a bag of keywords, the system tries to name the underlying task: what information should be retrieved or what action should be supported. The abstract says this extraction is multi-stage and iterative, with a closed-source language model working with a lightweight agent, so the process likely alternates between stronger understanding and cheaper agent adaptation. The next stage uses the captured intent as a design target. The system looks for or defines an API that would make the intent solvable in the real map service, keeping the user context in view rather than designing a tool in isolation. Then it generates training pairs for that intent: example user requests paired with the intended API-using behavior. These examples are not accepted wholesale. A two-stage filtering module selects the most influential data points for fine-tuning, meaning the training set is compressed toward examples expected to change the agent’s behavior most usefully. The output is a map-guide agent that has learned a newly discovered API with less direct human authoring.
math: The main mathematical idea is learning from examples: the agent must learn a mapping from a user request to an intent and then from that intent to an API-using action. In plain terms, it is being shown many cases until it can repeat the pattern on a new case. A second idea is matching. Each intent is like a job description, and each API is like a machine that can perform some jobs but not others; the system must decide whether the job and the machine fit. A third idea is filtering under uncertainty. Generated training pairs vary in usefulness, so the system needs a scoring process that separates examples likely to teach the agent from examples that may add noise. Fine-tuning is the act of adjusting the agent after seeing selected examples so that future choices move toward the selected behavior. The tradeoff is labor versus trust. Generating and filtering examples saves human effort, but it depends on the scoring process recognizing which examples carry real signal. The paper also uses iteration: repeated passes can correct coarse intent guesses before they become API designs.
dots: This paper sits with other conference work on language-model agents, tool use, retrieval, and learning from generated supervision. Its surface setting is Baidu Map, but the deeper problem is common: a model that speaks naturally must act through structured services, and those services are incomplete when user needs change. That connects it to ranking and matching because the system must choose which API fits an intent. It connects to information retrieval because the API is a route to current external facts rather than knowledge stored inside the model. It also connects to self-supervised or self-instruct data generation, where a system creates training examples from its own reasoning and then filters them. Neighboring papers on SQL checking or biomedical screening share the same pressure: use a strong language model to create or judge training signal, then train a smaller or more specialized component for dependable deployment.
ww: ARADD should improve over the manual or rule-based approach because it starts from actual query logs, where unmet needs appear before engineers have named them. If many users ask for a task that the current agent handles poorly, intent extraction can turn those requests into a candidate capability. The multi-stage setup helps because intent is not a single word; it is the practical reason behind the request. A stronger language model can help identify that reason, while the lightweight agent can absorb the final pattern for cheaper service use. Context-aware API design matters because an API is only useful if it matches the real setting where the request appears. Self-instruct training then creates many ways to express the same new intent, giving the agent more than one phrasing to learn from. Filtering is the trust step: it reduces the chance that weak generated pairs dominate training. The system works when these stages reinforce one another: real demand guides intent, intent guides API design, and filtered examples guide fine-tuning.
po: The payoff is a faster path from new user demand to a usable AI Guide capability in Baidu Map. The abstract claims ARADD can discover real-world APIs suitable for solving queries and master them with minimal labor cost. It also reports validation on a real-world log dataset and in the online service side, which matters because API discovery is a production workflow, not just an offline text task. If the pipeline is reliable, the map assistant can cover a wider variety of user intents without waiting for extensive manual labeling and hand-designed training data.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The query logs must contain enough repeated evidence to reveal real new intents, and the intent extractor must distinguish a genuinely new need from unusual wording of an old one. The generated training pairs must describe valid API use, not plausible but wrong behavior. The filtering module must be good at selecting influential examples without discarding rare but important cases. The abstract does not prove how well ARADD handles unsafe API designs, changing API behavior, conflicting intents, or domains outside Baidu Map. It also gives the high-level modules, but not enough detail here to judge failure recovery when a discovered API is only partly suitable.
